@@114802940 <h> Political lessons from past public sector reforms <p> The world has moved on from the 1980s and new challenges also need to be addressed , says Andrew Podger . ( Zennie/Private Media ) <p> article-body <p> As The Mandarin celebrates its 10th anniversary , it is perhaps timely to look back to consider lessons from previous reform eras as well as forward to where public sector reform should be heading now . <p> For the Albanese government , facing criticisms for timidity , revisiting the processes successfully used by the Hawke government may provide guidance on how to gain political credit while also delivering substantial and lasting reform . <p> For the Coalition , there may also be lessons from how Labor in opposition in 1982 laid the groundwork for Hawke 's machinery of government reforms which helped it in government to deliver its wider reforms . Noting these were largely maintained by the Howard government . <p> For Katy Gallagher in particular , the political success of Joe Dawkins -- like her finance minister and minister for the public service but later minister for education and employment then treasurer -- suggests that bold reform , carefully developed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The Hawke government 's public service and budget reforms in 1984 were guided by the 1976 Coombs royal commission , the 1982 Reid Review of Commonwealth Administration and the 1982 JCPAA ( Connolly ) report on the selection and development of senior managers . From these came the 1982 ' Labor and Quality in Government ' document as part of Labor 's election platform . <p> In government , Dawkins set up and chaired a committee that included the PM&amp;C secretary and representatives from the Public Service Board and the Department of Finance . This committee was supported by a small group of officials who worked full-time to develop specific proposals for the committee 's consideration , collaborating closely with the board and finance . <p> Within a couple of months , Dawkins obtained cabinet endorsement for a white paper on public service reform . It was published at the end of 1983 as a basis for consultation and negotiation , including with unions . Subsequently , at the end of March 1984 , cabinet agreed to a comprehensive range of legislative proposals including : <p> new provisions for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ reduction in hierarchies by abolishing the public service divisional structure and requiring agencies to plan for greater staff participation in decision-making , <p> rebadging the former second division as the Senior Executive Service with wider responsibilities as a leadership cadre , <p> the Members of Parliament ( Staff ) Act , <p> the creation of a new statutory authority to deal with grievances and appeals , <p> a statement of merit principles , and <p> a requirement for agencies to develop plans for equal employment opportunity and permanent part-time work . <p> Enabling legislation was passed shortly thereafter , about eight months after Dawkins established his committee . <p> In April 1984 , Dawkins released a second white paper , this time on budget reform . The measures included publication of the forward estimates , a central role for the Expenditure Review Committee of cabinet , annual strategy meetings of cabinet , the introduction of program budgeting with accountability to the Parliament for results and regular evaluations of programs against their objectives , the merger of staff and budget controls , the beginning of running cost reforms ( devolving financial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ caps ) , and the establishment of the financial management improvement program . <p> These reforms were later complemented by measures on the accountability of statutory authorities and GBEs to promote their efficient and effective operation ( the 1986 ' Walsh Rules ' , which were foreshadowed in the two white papers ) and the 1987 portfolio restructuring . They laid the framework for the new public service and financial management legislation finally enacted in the late 1990s under Howard . <p> Importantly , the reforms were not just about obscure HRM and financial management initiatives but laid the foundation for the Hawke government to develop its overall priorities and strategic direction , to form a strong partnership with the public service to clarify and deliver those policies , and to ensure the efficient and effective management of its programs . <p> The vast majority of the changes proved successful . They gave the government and ministers greater control without curbing the professional independence and non-partisanship of the public service ; cabinet processes were rigorous and disciplined ; the government and ministers were better able to draw on the expertise @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ improved efficiency and effectiveness of government administration ; they also improved openness and accountability to the Parliament ; and they led over time to a far more representative public service , especially for women . <p> With the benefit of hindsight , however , some of the shifts that these measures started subsequently went too far . Tenure for secretaries was removed in 1993 ; ministerial staff were no longer expert consultants and public servants on secondment but political apprentices whose role was increasingly to control the APS ; devolution was unwisely extended to pay and conditions in the late 1990s ; the efficiency agenda became dominated by the use of competition with contracting out undermining internal capability ; and the new PSC lacked the authority of the former PSB to provide the professional leadership the APS requires . <p> Some important reforms were also allowed to wither . Evaluations of programs became a rarity rather than a standard requirement ; program performance information has deteriorated rather than improved ; portfolio structures which originally set clear lines of accountability and facilitated the operation of a manageable cabinet have become a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and too many ministers having responsibilities in multiple portfolios ; the idea of annual cabinet strategy meetings never really got off the ground , more 's the pity . <p> Repairing these excesses and lost opportunities should represent a substantial reform agenda by itself . But the world has moved on from the 1980s and new challenges also need to be addressed . <p> These include taking far more advantage of technology advances to improve service delivery ( and policy analysis and advice ) , rethinking the way to invest in technology ( avoiding the sorts of pressures that contributed to robodebt ) , looking afresh at partnerships with the states in areas such as health , education , housing and urban development , and addressing the implications for public sector management . <p> While the Albanese government has made some progress in some areas such as winding back excessive reliance on contractors and consultants , its timidity has been revealed in the disappointing amendments to the PS Act this year that omitted key recommendations from Thodey which the robodebt royal commission endorsed . <p> With this term in office @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of more substantial legislation being introduced for consideration by this Parliament . So , what might Katy Gallagher do now ? <p> Her annual speech on APS reform towards the end of this year provides an opportunity for her to foreshadow in more detail what a second Albanese government plans to do and how she sees those reforms contributing to improvements in wider policy and administration such as in national security , climate change , education , health and social inclusion . <p> With the support of the prime minister , she might commit a new Labor government not only to a highly active cabinet , but also to machinery of government changes designed for the next decade or more . These might include a portfolio structure with clear lines of accountability to cabinet and its committees , supporting a highly disciplined approach to priority setting , and also facilitating a more stable basis for working with the APS on long-term strategic policies and the effective and efficient management of ongoing Commonwealth functions ( such as immigration ) and functions where the Commonwealth must work in partnership with the states @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the proposals set out in my recent discussion paper , promising legislation to lock in the reforms . Some require further work and public consultation , so she could ask the APS Commission and the secretaries ' board to prepare public discussion papers ( for example , on a clearer framework for the APS values that could be used to articulate the respective roles and values of other Commonwealth employees ) . <p> But the reforms could go further , particularly on the use of technology and on partnerships that can deliver services responsive to individual and community needs and preferences . <p> My suspicion is that Gallagher has relied too much on the APS Commission to give her reform options . She might grab hold of the reins herself as she prepares for an election and ( she hopes ) a new term in government . <p> Perhaps , like Labor in 1982 , she could find some external advisers to help her . Or like Dawkins in 1983 , she could set up and chair a dedicated committee supported by a small taskforce working briefly but full-time on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ PM&amp;C . These might draw on Thodey , the robodebt royal commission , the other recent royal commissions on aged care and disability services , and the many recent parliamentary inquiries . <p> The Coalition should also be reflecting on lessons from its own experience in government , recognising that public service failures hurt them politically . And carefully examining the various inquiry reports around . <p> Its policy agenda needs a capable and confident public service . It needs to develop machinery of government reforms that promote quality decision-making by ministers and high performance by the public service . <p> Andrew Podger AO is a professor of public policy at Australian National University . In his public service career , Andrew served as the Australian Public Service Commissioner and as departmental secretary for federal departments , including Arts and Administrative Services , Housing and Regional Development , and Health and Family Services .

@@114846321 <h> How Google are Using AI to Track Whales <p> By Doccy Darko <p> Today <p> Credit Dr Lauren Harrell <p> A unique new partnership that combines marine research with Google AI technology will enhance researchers ' understanding of humpback whale behaviours , migration patterns and marine habitats.Google 's Digital Future Initiative is supporting whale researchers Dr Olaf Meynecke from Griffith University 's Whales and Climate Program and Dr Lauren Harrell from Google Research to more precisely , efficiently and comprehensively monitor whale migrations and their ecosystems along Australia 's East Coast with the deployment of hydrophones -- and with automatic audio detection , powered by Google AI . <p> Monitoring the sounds and songs of humpback whales is a helpful indicator of ecosystem health . It can help scientists understand migration activity , patterns , mating calls and competitive behaviours . Traditional whale research methods typically involved painstaking and laborious processes such as logging sightings of whales , and manually reviewing audio data . Additionally , whale sighting data can only be gathered during daylight , so scientists were not previously able to collect detailed , comprehensive data over continuous stretches of time . <p> The hydrophones and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ automatic and continuous audio data collection and analysis . Hydrophones are microphones used underwater for recording or listening to underwater sounds , and their use in this particular project will support whale sightings from boats and land . <p> " Hydrophones allow us to tune into marine soundscapes 24/7 , " Dr Meynecke said . " The Whales and Climate Program currently holds the largest whale sighting database in Australia but this is sighting data captured during the daytime , which means there is no data spanning 24-hour periods . " The hydrophone array will help us to capture continuous data over the course of a 24-hour period and do this for the entire whale season every year . We will be collecting many terabytes of acoustic data that then will be analysed with Google 's AI technology to detect whale location and activity . We can then match that data with existing visual sightings , providing a much more holistic picture of whale movements and behaviours . " <p> Three hydrophones have already been deployed off the Gold Coast , Sydney and Merimbula , with at least another three @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ at approximately 500km intervals , ensuring wide coverage of annual migrations that typically span the Australian east coast . <p> The project is enabled by the Digital Future Initiative , Google Australia 's $1 billion investment in Australian research , partnerships and infrastructure . This commitment supports a range of AI-focused projects across healthcare , sustainability , energy and more -- including A2O Search , a search engine for bird and wildlife sounds . <p> Advertisement <p> Advertisement <p> " We 're delighted to partner with Griffith University to give researchers new AI tools so they can gain a richer and more comprehensive understanding of humpback whales , underwater ecosystems and the impact of climate change , " said Dr Harrell , data scientist at Google Research . <p> " Google 's AI technology detects whale sounds , marks the location in time and classifies the species .
